extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline (OED) staff, and attorneys involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, and factors the USPTO (and its Director/ALJ) use to evaluate alleged misconduct by persons practicing before the Office and to determine appropriate sanctions. Covers specific disciplinary rules, filing requirements on appeal, statute-of-limitations rules, and aggravating/mitigating considerations for sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client about correspondence (37 C.F.R. §10.23(a),(b); 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the client of important Office correspondence; not merely 'notify' but 'inform' about the correspondence and its ramifications so the client can make an informed decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing duty to inform (continuing violations doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to inform the client of potentially adverse information remains active until the practitioner informs the client of the correspondence or ceases representation of that client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the duty is continuing, failure to fully inform may be treated as ongoing misconduct; the statute of limitations may run from the time the duty ended (e.g., when representation was severed) or when the misconduct was made known to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect / failure to act with reasonable diligence (37 C.F.R. §10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not neglect a client's matter and must act with reasonable diligence; failing to monitor appeals, failing to respond to examiner's communications, or allowing a matter to languish can constitute neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example facts cited: failure to monitor the appeal status, failure to contact the examiner in 2009, and failure to take steps to confirm the application's status in 2010–2011 — all supported a finding of neglect under §10.77(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligent prosecution / monitoring of patent applications (37 C.F.R. §10.84(a)(1) & (2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must diligently prosecute patent applications and properly monitor prosecution (e.g., responses to Office Actions, appeals deadlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ found violation of §10.84(a)(1) & (2) where the practitioner neglected the '519 Application from May 2006 until October 2011 by failing to monitor and manage prosecution, resulting in abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to return client property / file (37 C.F.R. §10.112(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon request, a practitioner must return the client's file and property unless a valid retaining lien exists; retaining the file without legal basis is a disciplinary violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order held that EPRT was entitled to the file because no retaining lien existed; Appellant's failure to return the file upon request violated §10.112(c)(4). Practitioner’s loss or misplacement of the file is not an adequate excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate and respond to client inquiries (related to §§10.23, 10.77)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep clients reasonably informed and must respond to reasonable client requests for information in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal to communicate — e.g., failing to answer repeated emails, texts, and phone calls over extended periods — was treated as intentional misconduct supporting sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate docketing and office procedures (practical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must maintain reliable office and docketing systems (tickler, calendar, customer number association, mail-handling) to ensure receipt and timely handling of Office correspondence/deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ cited an inadequate manual tickler system, reliance on a receptionist/ex-wife, failure to associate USPTO Customer Number with the application, and improper mail handling as evidence of negligence contributing to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with USPTO Director appeal filing requirements (37 C.F.R. §11.55; FRAP 28/32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal briefs to the USPTO Director must comply with 37 C.F.R. §11.55 and the substantive requirements of FRAP 28(a)(2),(3),(5)-(10) and 32(a)(4)-(6): include appellant's contentions with reasons and citations, concise statement of applicable standard of review, statement of the case, statement of facts, summary of argument, issues presented, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncompliant briefs (missing required sections, failing to identify record citations, incorporating facts into arguments to circumvent page limits) may be struck or provide independent basis to reject the appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction and authority (35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2)(D); 35 U.S.C. §32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has statutory authority to promulgate regulations governing conduct of persons practicing before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners shown to be incompetent, disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners registered before the Office are bound by USPTO disciplinary rules and are subject to suspension/exclusion under these statutes and implementing regulations (37 C.F.R. §§10.xx / 11.xx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for disciplinary proceedings (35 U.S.C. §32 as amended — AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proceeding must be commenced not later than the earlier of 10 years after the misconduct or 1 year after the misconduct is made known to an officer or employee of the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of the two-stage rule may be influenced by the continuing-violations doctrine (duty continuing until client informed or representation ends); misconduct that occurred prior to applicable cutoffs may be time-barred under earlier statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors under 37 C.F.R. §11.54(b) and ABA Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, the Director/ALJ considers the violations proven together with the factors listed in §11.54(b) and ABA Standards: nature/seriousness of violation, whether actions were intentional/knowing/negligent, prior disciplinary history, amount of actual/potential injury to client, and aggravating/mitigating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explicitly relied on these factors and ABA 'Standards For Imposing Lawyer Sanctions' guidance in selecting an 8‑month suspension conditioned on passing the MPRE and satisfying reinstatement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (examples used to increase sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of aggravating factors include prior disciplinary history, obstruction of investigations (e.g., settlement clause preventing testimony), obstinate refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, seniority/experience (greater experience can aggravate), abusive conduct toward participants, and refusal/failure to make restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ listed these factors and treated them as increasing the appropriate sanction; prior similar discipline and attempts to silence witnesses were considered especially serious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible mitigating factors include personal or mental health circumstances and absence of dishonest motive (no greed or nefarious intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ considered personal circumstances and lack of dishonest motive as mitigating but found them insufficient to outweigh aggravating factors and prior history in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on obstructing disciplinary investigations (37 C.F.R. §11.304(f) and related principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not act in bad faith to hinder or derail disciplinary investigations; contractual provisions intended to silence witnesses or prevent cooperation may constitute obstruction and an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The settlement clause prohibiting EPRT personnel from voluntarily participating in investigations was treated as bad-faith obstruction and increased sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparators / consistency of sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Director may compare the case to prior disciplinary matters to determine whether the selected sanction is within the established range for similar misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cited prior USPTO disciplinary decisions (e.g., 6‑month, 24‑month, 36‑month suspensions in similar neglect/abandonment/failed-communication cases) to support that an 8‑month suspension was within range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of suspension and requirements for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions may include suspension for a fixed period and conditions for reinstatement (e.g., passage of the MPRE, compliance with duties under 37 C.F.R. §11.58), dissociation from Customer Numbers/PKI, and notification to disciplinary authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order required an eight-month suspension, conditioned reinstatement upon passage of the MPRE, dissociation from Customer Numbers, prohibition on obtaining a Customer Number until reinstated, and compliance with duties of disciplined practitioners under §11.58.
